title: Offer Strategy & Negotiation for Investment Property

slides.title: Set your walk-away price from conservative NOI before you see the seller's number
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.8. Offer Strategy & Negotiation for Investment Property
meta: Education only. Not legal, lending, or real estate advice. Contracts are state-specific.
slides.notes:
This lesson is about one number you set before you ever talk to the seller: your walk-away price.

By the end you'll build that number from three things. Conservative net operating income. Your loan terms. And the cash you actually have. Then you'll learn the contract terms that protect it: earnest money, contingencies, appraisal gap, seller concessions, closing date, and furniture.

And you'll learn a habit. Every negotiation decision gets recorded as proceed, renegotiate, or walk, with the reason in one line.

We stay with Cedar Ridge. The asking price is $399,000. Maya and Chris end up under contract at $385,000. You'll see exactly why $399,000 fails their tests and $385,000 passes. All Cedar Ridge figures are assumptions from our canonical example.

slides.title: Decide the most you'll pay first, then negotiate below that number

nodes.d: Base cash flow, weak-case survival, cash
The lowest of the three ceilings
Seller won't go under? You walk, and you know why.

box.label: This fails if
box.text: You start from the $399,000 asking price, then nudge the nightly rate up until the spreadsheet works. Now the offer rests on the most optimistic line in the model.

slides.notes:
The asking price is the seller's opening position. It tells you what the seller hopes to get. It says nothing about what the house can carry as a rental.

A common way STR offers go wrong is working backward from the asking price. The buyer sees $399,000, then nudges the nightly rate up until the spreadsheet works. Now the offer depends on the most optimistic line in the model.

Reverse the order. Decide the most you'll pay first, from numbers you'd defend to a lender. Then negotiate below that number. If the seller won't come under it, you walk, and you already know why.

Sam's PA.4 lesson builds the underwriting package: revenue, expenses, cap rate, and cash-on-cash. I'm not redoing that here. What you bring back from PA.4 is two lines: base-case NOI and weak-case NOI. This lesson turns those two lines into a price.

slides.title: Your walk-away price is the lowest of three ceilings, run on the costlier loan
rows: At expected revenue, does the house clear a minimum cash flow after the loan?
In a weak year, does it break even, or is the shortfall funded in writing?
Shortfall up to $6,000 a year, two years set aside
Does everything you put in, plus your reserves, fit in the cash you have?
Inside $210,000, with $30,000 emergency fund and 6 months PITIA
slides.caption: They underwrite on the DSCR quote (7.25%, 1 point, 25% down) until the conventional approval is in writing. The three rules are theirs to set, so they're assumptions.
slides.notes:
Your walk-away price is the lowest of three ceilings.

Test one is base-case cash flow. At your expected revenue, the house must produce at least a minimum annual cash flow after the loan payment. You set the minimum. It should be more than zero, because base-case years still bring surprises.

Test two is weak-case survival. In a weak year, the house should break even. If it can't, you need a written, funded plan for the shortfall. A buyer who can't fund a weak year should hold the strict breakeven line.

Test three is cash. Down payment, closing costs, points, furnishing, lender reserves, a weak-year reserve, and your emergency fund. It all has to fit.

Use the more expensive financing quote for all three. That's the DSCR quote for Maya and Chris.

Why cash flow and not cap rate? Cap rate uses NOI but ignores your loan. Cash flow shows what the loan does to that NOI.

slides.title: Keeping $5,000 of base-case cash flow caps Cedar Ridge's price at $394,310

lines.label: Base-case NOI (tax and insurance already inside)
Loan as a share of price (25% down)

slides.side: NOI already covers property tax ($3,850) and insurance ($3,200), so cash flow is NOI minus principal and interest.
slides.notes:
Canonical inputs: base-case NOI $29,209, weak-case NOI $18,162. Property tax and insurance are already inside NOI. Maya and Chris have $210,000 in liquid savings.

Test one. Because NOI already covers tax and insurance, cash flow is simply NOI minus principal and interest.

They want at least $5,000 a year in the base case. So the most principal and interest they can carry is $29,209 minus $5,000. That's $24,209 a year, or $2,017 a month.

At 7.25% over 30 years, $2,017 a month supports a loan of about $295,732.

With 25% down, the loan is 75% of the price. Divide by 0.75 and the price ceiling is $394,310.

I ran every step in Python. On your own deal, a lender's calculator or a spreadsheet PV function does the same job. We'll get to that in the worksheet.

slides.title: A strict weak-case breakeven caps the price at $295,818, far below asking

lines.label: Weak-case NOI = max annual P&I at breakeven
Loan as a share of price

side_box.label: More cash doesn't close the gap
side_box.text: At $385,000, a breakeven loan means $163,137 down, 42.4% of price. Add closing costs and $32,000 furnishing, and $210,000 is gone.

slides.notes:
Test two, strict version. Breakeven in the weak case means principal and interest can't be more than weak-case NOI.

So the most they can carry is $18,162 a year. That supports a loan of about $221,863. Divide by 0.75 and the price ceiling is $295,818.

That's $103,182 under the asking price.

Could more cash close the gap instead? Let's check. At $385,000, a breakeven loan of $221,863 means a down payment of $163,137. That's 42.4% of the price. Add closing costs and the $32,000 furnishing budget, and their $210,000 is gone.

So under the strict rule, Cedar Ridge doesn't work anywhere near the asking price. That's a real answer, and for many buyers it's the right one. Hold on to it. On the next slide, Maya and Chris make a different choice, on purpose, and in writing.

slides.title: The lowest ceiling, the funded weak-case test, sets the walk-away price at $393,000
slides.caption: Funded version: max P&I = $18,162 + $6,000 = $24,162, so the ceiling is $393,544. Round down to $393,000. The strict test applies to buyers who can't fund a weak year.
slides.notes:
Maya and Chris have two W-2 incomes and savings. So they decide, in writing, that they can carry a weak-year shortfall of up to $6,000 a year. And they set aside two years of it.

That changes Test two. The most principal and interest they'll carry becomes $18,162 plus $6,000, which is $24,162. The price ceiling becomes $393,544.

Test three asks the highest price where all their cash needs stay at or under $210,000. That's 25% down, 3% closing costs, one point, $32,000 furnishing, six months of PITIA, two years of weak-case shortfall, and the $30,000 emergency fund. Python finds it at about $409,984.

Now take the lowest of the three that applies to them: $393,544, just under Test one's $394,310. Round down to $393,000.

That's a real choice, and they're making it on purpose. A buyer without their income or savings should use the strict test and pass on this house.

slides.title: At $399,000 both cash-flow tests fail; at $385,000 both pass
slides.caption: DSCR quote. At $399,000, base cash flow is under $5,000 and the weak shortfall is over $6,000.

box.label: Before you finalize
box.text: The model holds property tax at $3,850. Some counties reassess after a sale. Ask your agent or the county assessor what the tax would be at your price.

slides.notes:
Here's the same check at four prices, all on the DSCR quote.

At $399,000, the asking price, the loan is $299,250. Base cash flow is $4,712, under their $5,000 minimum. The weak shortfall is $6,335, over their $6,000 limit. Both tests fail.

At $392,000, both pass, barely. Keep that row in mind. It shows up in the negotiation later.

At $385,000, the eventual contract price, base cash flow is $5,572 and the weak shortfall is $5,475. Both pass with some room.

At $372,000, their opening offer, the numbers are better again.

One caution before you lock your ceiling. The model holds property tax at $3,850. Some counties reassess after a sale, and the tax could rise. Ask your agent or the county assessor what the tax would be at your price. A higher tax lowers NOI, and that lowers every ceiling.

slides.title: At $385,000, Maya and Chris commit $198,980 and keep $11,020 unallocated
rows: Total cash in (cash to close + furnishing)
slides.caption: Every line has a job. The unallocated $11,020 is the only slack in the plan.
slides.notes:
Here's what the cash plan looks like at $385,000.

Total cash in, which is cash to close plus furnishing, is $142,688. Lender reserves at six months of PITIA are $15,342. The weak-year reserve is two years of the $5,475 weak-case shortfall, so $10,950. And their personal emergency fund stays at $30,000, untouched.

Total committed: $198,980. Unallocated from their $210,000: $11,020.

I want you to notice what this table does. Every dollar has a job before they sign. The weak-year reserve isn't a hope. It's a line with a number on it.

And that $11,020 is the only slack in the whole plan. Keep an eye on it. In a few slides we'll hit a low appraisal and an inspection finding. That's when this number decides whether they proceed, renegotiate, or walk.

slides.title: Seven contract terms decide how much risk you carry between signing and closing

When it's at risk. Bigger deposit, bigger possible loss.
Days to inspect, then cancel or renegotiate
Long enough for STR insurance quotes and a licensing answer
Cancel if the loan isn't approved by a date
Match the lender's real timeline, with room to switch
Renegotiate or cancel on a low value; a gap clause covers some shortfall
Only offer gap cash you counted in Test 3
Seller credit toward your closing costs
The lender's dollar limit for this occupancy type
Sets your rate lock and launch timing
Lock expiry, extension cost, launch season
Items or reservations that come with the house
Fit, condition, lender treatment, platform transfer rules
slides.caption: Purchase contracts are state-specific. Treat these as questions for your agent and attorney, not rules.
slides.notes:
Price is one term. These decide how much risk you carry between signing and closing. Purchase contracts are state-specific, often a standard form your agent uses. So treat all of this as questions for your agent and attorney.

Earnest money counts toward your cash to close. A bigger deposit can make an offer stronger. It also raises what you could lose if you miss a deadline.

The inspection period is where you test the business, not just the house: permits, HOA rules, insurance quotes, septic capacity. PA.9 builds that list.

Lenders generally size the loan on the lower of price or appraised value. Ask yours to confirm. If you offer gap coverage, only offer cash you already counted in Test three.

Seller credits reduce your cash to close, but lenders limit them. Get the limit in dollars first.

For furniture, ask if it fits your OP.6 design plan, and how your lender treats it. For existing bookings, ask whether the platform even allows a transfer.

slides.title: Get written answers from your agent and lender before you shorten any contingency

left.head: Ask your agent
items: Can we still fit the inspection, septic or sewer check, and STR insurance quote?
What happens to my earnest money if I cancel after this expires?
What's normal here for this type of house?
Can the permit answer arrive before inspection ends?

right.head: Ask your lender
items: How many days do you really need to approve this loan?
What happens if the appraisal comes in $10,000 low?
Does approval depend on proof of STR permit eligibility?
What's your seller credit limit for this occupancy?
When does my rate lock expire, and what does extending cost?

box.label: Keep the contingency if
box.text: Any answer puts your earnest money at risk for a problem you can't test in time.

slides.notes:
Sellers sometimes ask for a shorter inspection period, no financing contingency, or appraisal gap coverage. Before you agree, get written answers to these questions.

From your agent: can you still fit the inspection, the septic or sewer check, and the STR insurance quote in a shorter window? What happens to your earnest money if you cancel after the contingency expires? What's normal in this market for this type of house? And can the permit or licensing answer arrive before inspection ends?

From your lender: how many days does it really need? What happens if the appraisal comes in $10,000 low? Does approval depend on proof of STR permit eligibility, and when? What's the seller credit limit? And when does the rate lock expire?

The rule is simple. If any answer puts your earnest money at risk for a problem you can't test in time, keep the contingency.

slides.title: A $375,000 appraisal means split the gap at most, or walk above $380,000
slides.text: The lender lends 75% of the lower value: $281,250, which is $7,500 less than planned. Their rule: keep at least $10,000 unallocated.
slides.caption: The smaller loan lowers PITIA to $2,506. Base cash flow rises to $6,186 and the weak case to -$4,861 in every option.

box.label: Decision
box.text: Renegotiate. Ask for $375,000. Accept up to $380,000. If the seller holds at $385,000 with the appraisal contingency open, walk.

slides.notes:
Two practice scenarios, both what-ifs on the accepted $385,000 contract. I've added one more rule for Maya and Chris: keep at least $10,000 of the $210,000 unallocated after every commitment. That's an assumption.

Scenario one: the appraisal comes in at $375,000. The lender lends 75% of the lower value, which is $281,250. That's $7,500 less than planned.

If they pay the full gap at $385,000, unallocated cash drops to $5,130. That breaks their rule. If they split the gap at $380,000, they keep $10,280. If the seller drops to $375,000, they keep $15,430.

The smaller loan helps cash flow in every option. Base rises to $6,186 and the weak case improves to minus $4,861.

Decision: renegotiate. Ask for $375,000. Accept anything up to $380,000. If the seller holds at $385,000 and the appraisal contingency is still open, walk. They'd be spending their margin on a price the appraiser didn't support.

slides.title: Absorbing $4,500 of repairs would drop unallocated cash to $6,520, so renegotiate

lines.label: Water heater and soft deck boards (assumption)

slides.side: That's under their $10,000 rule. Ask the seller to repair before closing or cut the price. Ask the lender first whether a seller credit can cover repairs. Guest safety items get fixed before launch either way (PA.12).

side_box.label: A different finding, a different answer
side_box.text: A septic system sized for fewer guests than planned can break the business plan. Walk unless the fix and the permit both work on paper.

slides.notes:
Scenario two: the inspection finds $4,500 of work. That's an assumption. Say the water heater is at the end of its life and several deck boards are soft.

If Maya and Chris absorb the cost, total committed rises from $198,980 to $203,480. Unallocated cash falls to $6,520. That's under their $10,000 rule.

Decision: renegotiate. Ask the seller to repair before closing, or to reduce the price. But ask the lender first whether a seller credit can go toward repairs or only toward closing costs. The answer changes what you ask the seller for.

If the finding is a safety issue for guests, it gets fixed before launch either way. PA.12 covers that sign-off.

Now notice the box. A different finding changes the answer. A failing septic system sized for fewer guests than you planned isn't a price problem. It can break the business plan. That's a walk unless the fix and the permit both work on paper.

slides.title: Give the seller what costs you little, and hold the terms that protect your ceiling
slides.caption: The seller accepts $385,000, which is $14,000 (3.5%) under asking. No seller credit, so cash to close stays $110,688. Terms are assumptions except the asking and contract prices.
slides.notes:
Here's how the Cedar Ridge negotiation could run. The terms are assumptions for teaching, except the asking and contract prices.

Round one: they offer $372,000. Why that number? It's $21,000 under their $393,000 walk-away price. That leaves room for two counters without crossing the line.

Round two: the seller counters at $392,000, 2% earnest money, a 7-day inspection, a 30-day close, and the furniture for $8,000 more. $392,000 is under their ceiling by only $1,000. It passes on paper with almost no margin. And the terms are the problem. Their agent says seven days isn't enough for the septic inspection and an STR insurance quote. Thirty days is tight for their lender. The furniture doesn't fit the OP.6 design plan, and in this mock their lender won't count it in the loan.

Round three: $385,000. They accept the larger deposit, which they'll put toward closing anyway. They hold inspection time, financing time, and the appraisal contingency. The seller accepts.

slides.title: Log every step as proceed, renegotiate, or walk, with a one-line reason tied to a test
rows: Inside ceiling by $1,000; inspection too short
slides.caption: All figures are assumptions from the Cedar Ridge example.
slides.notes:
This is Maya and Chris's decision log. Every event gets a date, the numbers, one of three decisions, and a one-line reason.

Look at the reasons column. None of them say "felt right" or "didn't want to lose the house." Every reason ties back to a test or a rule. $21,000 under walk-away. Inside the ceiling by only $1,000. Passes all three tests with $11,020 unallocated. The unallocated cash rule.

That's the point of the log. In the middle of a negotiation, emotions run high. You've already pictured the first guests. The log keeps you tied to the numbers you set when you were calm.

The last two rows are written before anything happens. They already know what they'll do if the appraisal comes in low or the inspection finds work. Decide your triggers in advance, too.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Fill in your inputs from PA.4, your costlier quote, and your own written rules
rows: Weak-case rule (breakeven or max funded shortfall)
slides.notes:
Now it's your turn. The exercise has three parts. This is part one: your inputs.

Use Sam's PA.4 numbers for base-case and weak-case NOI. Use your more expensive financing quote from PA.6 or PA.7 for the rate, term, points, and down payment. Closing costs come from your lender or agent. Furnishing comes from your OP.6 plan. Liquid cash comes from your actual bank statements, not a guess.

Then the four rules that are yours to set. Your minimum base-case cash flow. Your weak-case rule, either strict breakeven or a maximum funded shortfall. Your emergency fund. And the minimum cash you'll keep unallocated after every commitment.

Write those rules down before you look at any listing price. If you set them after, you'll set them to fit the house.

slides.title: Your walk-away price is the lowest of your three ceilings, rounded down
rows: (Base NOI minus minimum cash flow) → max loan at your rate → divide by loan-to-price
(Weak NOI plus allowed shortfall) → max loan → divide by loan-to-price
Highest price where total committed cash ≤ liquid cash
Lowest of the three, rounded down

box.label: Annual P&I to loan amount
box.text: Use your lender's calculator or a spreadsheet PV function: PV(rate/12, months, -monthly payment). Then part 2: write your offer terms. Part 3: keep the decision log.

slides.notes:
Here are the three ceilings, in formula form.

Test one: base NOI minus your minimum cash flow gives your maximum annual principal and interest. Turn that into a loan amount, then divide by your loan-to-price. At 25% down, that's 0.75.

Test two works the same way, starting from weak NOI plus your allowed shortfall. If you hold the strict rule, the allowed shortfall is zero.

Test three is the highest price where total committed cash stays at or under your liquid cash.

To turn a payment into a loan amount, use your lender's calculator or the PV function in a spreadsheet. PV of rate over 12, number of months, and the negative monthly payment.

Then part two: write your offer terms. Price, earnest money, each contingency and its days, any gap cap, seller concessions within the lender's limit, closing date, and included or excluded items. Part three is the decision log, from the first offer on.

slides.title: Six people confirm the pieces your walk-away price and contract depend on
rows: The local contract form, contingency periods, earnest money handling, and what's normal in this market.
What each contingency lets you do, when earnest money is at risk, and how any appraisal gap clause is worded.
Max seller credit for this occupancy, whether it can cover repairs, treatment of personal property, approval timeline, rate lock expiry.
The likely property tax at your purchase price.
An STR quote inside the inspection period.
That STR use is allowed at this address before the inspection contingency expires (SR.1).
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

Your real estate agent confirms the local contract form, the contingency periods, how earnest money is handled, and what's normal in this market.

Your attorney confirms what each contingency actually lets you do, when your earnest money is at risk, and how any appraisal gap clause is worded. Don't rely on my summary of any of that. Contracts are state-specific.

Your lender confirms the maximum seller credit for this occupancy type and whether it can cover repairs. It also confirms how personal property in the price is treated, the approval timeline, and when the rate lock expires.

The county assessor, or your agent, confirms the likely property tax at your price.

Your insurer gives you an STR quote inside the inspection period.

And the local licensing office confirms STR use is allowed at this address before the inspection contingency runs out. Use your SR.1 checklist.

slides.title: Write your walk-away price and your contract triggers before you make an offer
items: Write your four rules: minimum cash flow, weak-case rule, emergency fund, minimum unallocated cash.
Run the three ceilings on your costlier quote and write your walk-away price, rounded down.
Ask your agent and lender the contingency questions and save their answers in writing.
Start your decision log with your first offer and your appraisal and inspection triggers.
slides.next: Next: PA.9 Due Diligence: STR-Specific Inspections, Appraisal & Title Review. Bring your decision log.
slides.notes:
Four things this week, each under an hour.

First, write your four rules before you look at another listing. Minimum base-case cash flow, your weak-case rule, your emergency fund, and your minimum unallocated cash.

Second, run the three ceilings on your more expensive quote. Write the walk-away price, rounded down.

Third, send your agent and lender the contingency questions and keep their answers in writing.

Fourth, start your decision log. Put your first offer in it, and write your appraisal and inspection triggers before anything happens.

Maya and Chris now have an accepted contract at $385,000 and a 10-day inspection clock running. PA.9 fills that window: STR-specific inspections, the appraisal, and the title review, with a tracker that gives every item an owner and a deadline. Bring your decision log. Every finding in PA.9 gets a proceed, renegotiate, or walk entry.

slides.text: All ceilings, the four-price table, the cash plan, and both scenarios were computed in Python from the canonical Cedar Ridge inputs (Examples B1, B2, B4) on 2026-09-25.
slides.notes:
This lesson leans less on outside rules and more on arithmetic, so the source list is short.

The CFPB's Loan Estimate explainer supports one point. Your estimated cash to close includes the down payment and closing costs, minus any deposit already paid and any seller credits. That's why earnest money and seller concessions both show up in the cash plan.

The CFPB's guide to comparing loan offers is background for comparing terms before you commit.

The CFPB page on scheduling a home inspection is listed for the inspection versus appraisal distinction, which PA.9 develops. The lesson notes it wasn't independently opened.

Everything else, every ceiling, the four-price table, the cash plan, and both scenarios, was computed from the canonical Cedar Ridge inputs. Those are assumptions for teaching, not a real appraisal or quote.
